terms.grammar: adverb, and preposition with the accusative
evidence: Caes. BC 1.16.4: juxtā mūrum castra posuit (Lewis & Short)
Sall. Jug. 65.2: ut sellam juxtā pōneret
terms.comment: As an adverb, close by, at someone’s side: sellam juxtā pōnere. As a preposition it is not found before Caesar (Lewis & Short): juxtā focum, by the fire. Its other sense, “equally, just as” (juxtā ac sī), is not this one.

terms.grammar: preposition with the accusative; also an adverb, close by
evidence: Cic. Brut. 24: in prātulō propter Platōnis statuam cōnsēdimus
Ter. Ad. 170: hīc propter hunc adsiste
terms.comment: Rare but classical in this sense (Lewis & Short). Its everyday sense is “because of” (see due to), so keep it for a place plainly meant. For “by” a door or a gate, ad (see at); for “near”, prope.

phrases.latin: hīc propter hunc adsiste: em, sīc volō.
phrases.english: Stand here, next to him. There, that’s how I want it.

phrases.latin: tum in prātulō propter Platōnis statuam cōnsēdimus
phrases.english: then we sat down on a little lawn beside the statue of Plato

phrases.latin: ībat rēx obsitus aevō et comitem Aenēān juxtā nātumque tenēbat ingrediēns variōque viam sermōne levābat
phrases.english: the king, weighed down with years, walked on, keeping Aeneas and his son beside him, and lightened the way with talk

phrases.latin: mōre rēgum ut sellam juxtā pōneret
phrases.english: (he asked) to set his chair beside him, as kings do

phrases.latin: cētera intēctī tōtōs diēs juxtā focum atque ignem agunt
phrases.english: otherwise unclothed, they spend whole days by the hearth and the fire

juxta-u.against: the earlier draft of this record, jūxtā
juxta-u.html: Lewis & Short marks only the final ā, and the lexicon’s other records and the Latinitas loci write juxtā. De Vaan 318, s.v. juxta, derives it from Proto-Italic *jougVsto-, which would give a long u, but does not discuss the vowel. Left unmarked until it is settled.

Dickinson: Latin Core Vocabulary
